info.name: AI Backend Bootcamp
info.description:
Local test collection for the NestJS ai-backend-bootcamp API.

Run the API first:

    npm run start:dev

Base URL defaults to http://localhost:3000 (main.ts uses `process.env.PORT ?? 3000`).
Change the `baseUrl` collection variable if you set PORT in .env.

`POST /ai/chat` answers **201** on success. The success tests assert status and a
non-empty body only — the handler's return value is still changing as the AI
service gets wired up, so pinning exact text would make them break on every edit.
Each one logs the actual body to the Postman console so you can eyeball it.

Trimming is proved by the **whitespace-only** request instead: 8 spaces come back
400, which can only happen if @Transform ran before validation.

Validation failures answer 400 with the standard Nest shape:

    { "message": [ ...rule violations... ], "error": "Bad Request", "statusCode": 400 }

`POST /ai/chat` is behind `JwtAuthGuard` and needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
Both AI folders inherit that header from folder-level auth, filled from the
`accessToken` collection variable. A collection pre-request script obtains that
token once per run (register the shared test account, then log in), so every
folder can be run on its own and in any order.

Requires `JWT_SECRET` in .env — `JwtModule` uses `getOrThrow`, so the app will not
boot without it. `JWT_EXPIRES_IN` is optional and defaults to `1d`.

The Users folders create real accounts. Clean them up with:

    db.userdocuments.deleteMany({ email: /^register\./ })

Every request below was verified against a live server.

exec: // /ai/chat is behind JwtAuthGuard, and both AI folders inherit
// `Bearer {{accessToken}}` from their folder-level auth. This bootstraps that
// token once per run — register the shared test account (409 on later runs,
// which is fine) then log in — so any folder can be run on its own without
// first executing the Auth folder by hand.
body: jsonBody({ name: 'Postman User', email: creds.email, password: creds.password })

request.description: Sanity check that the server is up (AppController.getHello).

item.name: AI — valid requests
item.description:
POST /ai/chat is protected — AiController carries @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard).

Every request in this folder inherits the bearer token below, filled from the
`accessToken` collection variable that the collection pre-request script obtains.
See the 'AI — authentication' folder for what happens without it.

request.description: Happy path. The handler echoes back `body.message`.

The @Transform in ChatDto trims before validation runs.
The echoed response proves it: the surrounding spaces are gone.

ValidationPipe runs with { whitelist: true } but WITHOUT forbidNonWhitelisted,
so `role` and `isAdmin` are silently dropped rather than rejected.

Expect 201. If you later add forbidNonWhitelisted: true, this request starts
returning 400 instead — a useful decision to make deliberately.

exec: pm.test('status is 201 (extras stripped, not rejected)', function () {

item.name: AI — validation errors
item.description:
Same bearer token as the valid requests — these have to authenticate before the
DTO rules can be reached at all.

Nest runs guards BEFORE pipes, so an unauthenticated malformed body answers 401,
not 400. Getting 400 here is itself proof the guard let the request through.

request.description: Fails @MinLength(5).

Proves the @Transform trim actually runs before validation:
without it, 8 spaces would pass @MinLength(5).

exec: pm.test('status is 400 — trim ran before validation', function () {

request.description: Fails @IsNotEmpty and @MinLength(5).
No `message` key at all.
Fails @IsString. The @Transform passes non-strings through untouched.
Fails @MaxLength(4000). The 4001-char payload is generated by the pre-request script.

item.name: AI — authentication
item.description:
The rejection paths JwtAuthGuard introduces on POST /ai/chat.

Every request here sets `"auth": "noauth"` so it does NOT inherit the collection
token — each one supplies its own broken Authorization header, or none.

All of them carry a perfectly valid body. A 401 therefore proves the guard ran
before the ValidationPipe, which is the Nest execution order: guards, then
interceptors, then pipes.

Every request below was verified against a live server.

request.description: The endpoint used to be open. This is the request that proves it no longer is.

exec: pm.test('says the token is missing', function () {
pm.test('no model output leaked with the rejection', function () {

request.description:
A genuinely valid token sent under the wrong scheme.

JwtAuthGuard.extractToken only accepts `Bearer`, so this is treated as no token
at all rather than being verified anyway.

exec: pm.test('status is 401 even though the token itself is valid', function () {
pm.test('treated as missing, not as invalid', function () {

request.description:
Correct scheme, garbage token. verifyAsync throws and the guard converts it to a
generic 401 — expired, tampered and malformed tokens are deliberately
indistinguishable to the caller.

exec: pm.test('says the token is invalid', function () {
pm.test('no jsonwebtoken internals leak into the response', function () {

request.description:
Takes the real token and flips the last character of its signature.

The header and payload still decode cleanly, so this only fails if the signature
is actually being checked against JWT_SECRET — which is the whole point of the
guard. A 200 here would mean unsigned tokens are being trusted.

exec: pm.test('status is 401 — the signature is verified', function () {
pm.test('says the token is invalid', function () {

item.name: Users — valid requests
item.description:
POST /users/register creates an account.

These requests write to the real database the API is pointed at. The folder is
re-runnable: every account it creates uses an address generated in a pre-request
script (`register.<timestamp>.<n>@example.com`), so repeated runs never collide
with each other. Clean them up with:

    db.userdocuments.deleteMany({ email: /^register\./ })

Registration answers **201** — unlike login, it really does create a resource.

Every request below was verified against a live server.

request.description:
Happy path. UsersService.create checks the email is free, bcrypt-hashes the
password with 10 rounds, then inserts.

The generated address is kept in the `freshEmail` collection variable so the
duplicate-email request below can reuse it.

exec: pm.test('password is stored hashed, never in plain text', function () {
// KNOWN GAP, asserted so it stays visible rather than forgotten: the handler
// returns the raw mongoose document, so the bcrypt hash ships to the client.
// POST /auth/login does not do this — it builds its user object field by field.
// When register is given the same treatment, flip this to `.to.not.have.property`.
pm.test('KNOWN GAP: response still exposes the password hash', function () {

request.description:
Reuses the address the previous request just claimed.

UsersService.create finds the existing user and throws ConflictException, so the
caller gets a clean 409 instead of a raw E11000 duplicate-key error leaking out
of the unique index.

Run this request on its own and it will 404-free but 201 instead — it depends on
the request above having run first in the same session.

exec: pm.test('reports the conflict, not a driver error', function () {

item.name: POST /users/register —email is lowercased, name is trimmed

request.description:
The @Transform hooks in RegisterUserDto run before validation and before the
duplicate check.

That ordering is the point: UsersService.create looks the email up with a raw
findOne({ email }), and the schema's own `lowercase: true` only applies on save.
Without the DTO transform, 'Foo@Bar.com' would miss the stored 'foo@bar.com' and
hit the unique index as an unhandled E11000.

exec: pm.test('email was trimmed and lowercased', function () {

request.description:
ValidationPipe runs with { whitelist: true }, so anything not declared on
RegisterUserDto is dropped before the service sees it.

This is the request that matters most for the whitelist setting: `role` and
`isAdmin` are a mass-assignment attempt, and the injected `_id` tries to pin the
document id. All three should vanish.

Note there is no forbidNonWhitelisted, so extras are stripped silently rather
than rejected — expect 201, not 400.

exec: pm.test('status is 201 (extras stripped, not rejected)', function () {
pm.test('role and isAdmin never reached the document', function () {

item.name: Users — validation errors
item.description:
RegisterUserDto rules, each rejected by the global ValidationPipe with 400
before UsersService runs — so no duplicate lookup and no bcrypt hashing happen.

Failures use the standard Nest shape:

    { "message": [ ...rule violations... ], "error": "Bad Request", "statusCode": 400 }

Nothing here writes to the database, so this folder is safe to run repeatedly.

Every request below was verified against a live server.

request.description: Fails @MinLength(2).

Proves the name @Transform trim runs before validation: without it, 8 spaces
would sail past @MinLength(2) and create a user with a blank name.

exec: pm.test('status is 400 — trim ran before validation', function () {

request.description: Fails @IsEmail.
Fails @MinLength(8).

Fails @MaxLength(72). bcrypt silently ignores input past 72 bytes, so accepting
a longer password would quietly weaken it — rejecting is the honest answer.

The 73-character payload comes from the pre-request script.

Empty body. All three fields are reported at once — ValidationPipe collects
every violation rather than stopping at the first.

exec: pm.test('reports name, email and password together', function () {

request.description:
Fails @IsString / @IsEmail. The @Transform hooks pass non-strings through
untouched instead of throwing, so validation is what rejects them.

item.name: Usage
item.description:
Per-account spend reporting, all three behind JwtAuthGuard.

    GET /usage           raw records, date-filterable, paginated
    GET /usage/by-date   one row per UTC calendar day
    GET /usage/summary   grand totals plus a per-model breakdown

None of them takes a userId — every handler reads it from the verified token, so
there is no parameter through which one account could reach another's spend. The
'Usage — errors and access control' folder proves that.

The folder seeds its own data with a chat call, so it can be run on its own.

Costs are summed as floats and rounded to 6 decimal places, which is why totals
read 0.00135 rather than 0.0013500000000000003.

Every request below was verified against a live server.

request.description:
AiService writes a UsageRecord on every chat call — that write is what the
three reports below read.

The response tokens and cost are stashed so the assertions further down can check
the reports actually reflect this call rather than just returning plausible
numbers.

exec: // UTC because the daily rollup groups with $dateToString on an ISO date.

request.description:
Returns { items, total, limit, skip }. `total` counts everything matching the
filter, not just the current page, so a client can render pagination without a
second call.

Defaults are limit 20 / skip 0.

exec: pm.test('returns paging metadata alongside the items', function () {
pm.test('the seeded record is on top — sorted newest first', function () {
pm.test('every record belongs to the caller', function () {

request.description:
limit caps the page at 1 while `total` keeps reporting the full match count —
that difference is the thing worth asserting, since a count computed from the
page would silently break paging.

exec: pm.test('page holds one record but total counts them all', function () {

request.description:
One row per UTC calendar day, newest first, each carrying that day's request
count, token totals and cost.

Days are grouped in UTC, so a call made at 01:00 local time east of Greenwich
lands on the previous UTC day. That is deliberate — it keeps the boundary
stable regardless of who is asking.

exec: pm.test("today's row exists and counts the seeded call", function () {
pm.test('input and output tokens add up to the total', function () {
pm.test('rows are ordered newest day first', function () {

request.description:
Grand totals across the whole account, plus `byModel` sorted by spend so the
most expensive model is first — which is what you actually want to see when a
bill looks wrong.

exec: pm.test('totals include the seeded call', function () {
pm.test('cost is rounded, not raw float noise', function () {
pm.test('the seeded model appears in the breakdown', function () {
pm.test('byModel is ordered by spend, highest first', function () {
pm.test('first request is not after the last', function () {

item.name: GET /usage/summary —a bare `to` covers the whole day

request.description:
The subtle one. "2026-08-18" parses to midnight, so a naive $lte would exclude
everything that happened during that day and report zero for a range the caller
clearly meant to include.

The service stretches a date-only `to` to 23:59:59.999 UTC. A full timestamp is
honoured exactly as written instead.

This request asks for usage up to today and must see the record seeded minutes
ago. A zero here means the stretch was lost.

exec: pm.test("today's own records are inside a range ending today", function () {

item.name: GET /usage/summary —range with no usage returns zeroes

request.description:
An empty aggregation returns no rows at all. The service turns that into zeroes
rather than passing null through, so a client never has to special-case a quiet
period — the shape is identical to a busy one.

exec: pm.test('totals are zero rather than null', function () {
pm.test('the timestamps are null, not epoch zero', function () {

item.name: Usage — errors and access control
item.description:
What the reports refuse to do.

The access-control request is the important one: it logs in as a second,
freshly created account and asks for the first account's records by id. It must
come back empty — the query parameter is stripped by the ValidationPipe
whitelist, and the handler uses the token's `sub` regardless.

Every request below was verified against a live server.

item.name: GET /usage —another user cannot read your spend

request.description:
Run the Usage folder first so `usageUserId` holds a real account id with
records behind it.

The pre-request script registers a throwaway second account and logs in as it.
This request then presents that second token while explicitly asking for the
first account's userId.

Two layers have to fail for this to leak: ValidationPipe would have to keep an
undeclared query parameter, and UsageController would have to prefer it over
req.user.sub. Expect an empty page.

exec: body: jsonBody({ name: 'Other User', email: email, password: password })
body: jsonBody({ email: email, password: password })
pm.test('status is 200 — a valid token, just a different account', function () {
pm.test('sees none of the other account\'s records', function () {

request.description:
UsageController is guarded as a whole, so none of the three reports is reachable
anonymously.

exec: pm.test('says the token is missing', function () {

request.description: Confirms the guard sits on the controller rather than on the one handler.

Both dates are individually valid, so the DTO cannot catch this — the service
checks the pair and rejects it.

Without the check Mongo would happily match nothing and the caller would read an
empty result as 'no usage' instead of 'your range is backwards'.

exec: pm.test('status is 400, not an empty 200', function () {
pm.test('explains which way round the range should be', function () {

request.description:
Fails @IsDateString and @Max(100). The limit ceiling exists so a single request
cannot ask the database for an unbounded page.

Query strings arrive as text, so `limit` only validates as a number because the
DTO carries @Type(() => Number) and the pipe runs with transform: true.

exec: pm.expect(body).to.include('limit must not be greater than 100');

request.description:
Fails @Min(0). Mongo treats a negative skip as an error, so catching it at the
edge keeps a driver exception out of the response.

item.name: Auth
item.description:
POST /auth/login exchanges credentials for a JWT.

The folder is runnable standalone: the first request seeds the account it then
logs in with, and tolerates 409 so re-runs work.

Login answers **200**, not Nest's default 201 — @HttpCode(HttpStatus.OK) is on
the handler because signing in reads credentials rather than creating a resource.

On success the token is stashed in the `accessToken` collection variable, so
protected endpoints can send `Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}` once
JwtAuthGuard is applied to them.

Requires JWT_SECRET in .env — JwtModule uses getOrThrow, so the app refuses to
boot without it. JWT_EXPIRES_IN is optional and defaults to 1d.

Every request below was verified against a live server.

request.description:
Creates the account the login requests use.

201 on the first run, 409 on every run after — UsersService.create rejects a
duplicate email with ConflictException. Both are accepted here so the folder
stays re-runnable.

Happy path. Returns { accessToken, user: { id, name, email } }.

The password hash is never part of the response — AuthService builds the user
object field by field rather than spreading the mongoose document.

exec: pm.test('returns the user without the password hash', function () {
pm.test('token payload carries sub and email', function () {

request.description:
Proves the @Transform in LoginDto runs before the lookup.

The stored email is lowercase and findByEmail queries it raw, so without the
trim + lowercase this request would 401 instead of 200.

exec: pm.test('status is 200 — casing and padding were normalized', function () {
pm.test('resolved to the lowercase account', function () {

request.description: Real account, bad password. 401 with the generic 'Invalid credentials'.

No such account. Deliberately answers exactly like the wrong-password case —
a distinct 'user not found' would turn this endpoint into an account enumerator.

If this test ever fails, the two branches have drifted apart.

exec: pm.test('same message as a wrong password — no enumeration', function () {

request.description:
Fails @IsEmail and @MinLength(8) — rejected by ValidationPipe with 400 before
AuthService ever runs, so no database lookup and no bcrypt comparison happen.
Neither field present.
